prompt: Match each word to its meaning.

right.text: A flat surface of a solid
A line where two faces meet
The point where the triangular faces of a pyramid meet
A flat pattern that folds up to make a solid
The shape you see when you slice through a solid

hints: The plural of vertex is vertices.
solution: Face: flat surface. Edge: where two faces meet. Vertex: a corner. Apex: the top point of a pyramid. Net: flat pattern that folds into a solid. Cross-section: the shape of a slice.

prompt: Which of these solids is **not** a prism?

feedback.b: A cube has identical square ends joined by square faces, and the same cross-section all the way through, so it is a prism.
feedback.c: A cuboid is a rectangular prism.
feedback.d: It has two identical triangular ends joined by rectangles.

hints: A prism has the same cross-section all the way through.
solution: A **square-based pyramid** narrows to a point (the apex), so its cross-section changes. It is a pyramid, not a prism.

prompt: Select **all** the solids that are **pyramids**.
hints: A pyramid has a polygon base and flat triangular faces meeting at an apex.
A cone has a curved surface.
solution: The tetrahedron, square-based pyramid and hexagonal pyramid are pyramids. A cone has a circular base and a curved surface, so it is not a pyramid. A triangular prism is a prism.

prompt: A cylinder stands upright on one of its circular ends. What shape is its **plan view** (the view from directly above)?

feedback.b: A rectangle is what you see from the front or the side.
feedback.c: An oval appears when you look at the end at an angle. A plan view looks straight down.
feedback.d: There are no corners when you look down on a cylinder.

hints: Imagine looking straight down on a can of drink.
solution: Looking straight down you see the circular top, so the plan view is a **circle**. The front and side views are rectangles.

prompt: A square-based pyramid stands on its base. What does its **front view** look like?

options.text: A square with both diagonals drawn

feedback.b: This is the **plan view**: from above you see the square base with the four sloping edges meeting at the apex in the middle.
feedback.c: A plain square is what you would see from directly underneath. From the front, the sloping faces narrow to a point.
feedback.d: The faces narrow to a point, so the front view can't have a flat top.

hints: Imagine standing in front of the pyramid at ground level.
solution: From the front you see one triangular face rising from the base to the apex, so the front view is a **triangle**. The plan view is a square with its diagonals drawn.

prompt: For prisms and pyramids, faces + vertices − edges = 2 (Euler's rule). A solid has 7 faces and 15 edges. How many vertices does it have?
hints: Substitute into $F + V - E = 2$.
solution: $7 + V - 15 = 2$, so $V - 8 = 2$ and $V = 10$. (It is a pentagonal prism: 7 faces, 15 edges, 10 vertices.)

modelAnswer: If the row of four is folded into a loop, it makes four sides of the cube. Both extra squares stick out on the same side of the row, so when they fold in they cover the same open end of the loop. They overlap, and the other end of the cube is left without a face.

rubric.criterion: Recognises that the two extra squares fold onto the same face (they overlap)
States that this leaves one face of the cube open/missing

hints: Fold the row of four into a loop first. Where do the two extra squares go?
solution: The row of four squares folds round to make four sides of the cube. The two extra squares are both on the **same** side of the row, so they fold onto the **same** end of the cube and overlap. The opposite end is left open, so it is not a net of a cube.

prompt: Explain why every pyramid has the same number of faces as vertices.
modelAnswer: If the base has n sides, the pyramid has n triangular faces (one on each side of the base) plus the base, so n + 1 faces. It has n vertices around the base plus the apex, so n + 1 vertices. Both are n + 1, so they are always equal.

rubric.criterion: Shows faces = n + 1 (n triangles plus the base)
Shows vertices = n + 1 (n base corners plus the apex), so they are equal

hints: Let the base have $n$ sides. Count the faces, then count the vertices.
solution: With an $n$-sided base: faces $= n$ triangles $+ 1$ base $= n + 1$; vertices $= n$ base corners $+ 1$ apex $= n + 1$. They are always equal.

prompt: Which of these could be the number of edges of a prism?

feedback.b: A prism has $3n$ edges, so the number must be a multiple of 3. 25 isn't.

hints: If the end of a prism has $n$ sides, how many edges does the prism have?
solution: A prism with $n$-sided ends has $n$ edges on each end and $n$ joining them: $3n$ edges. So the number of edges must be a multiple of 3. Only **27** works ($n = 9$, a nonagonal prism).

prompt: A prism and a pyramid have the same number of edges. The pyramid's base has 9 sides. How many sides does each end of the prism have?
hints: A pyramid with an $n$-sided base has $2n$ edges.
A prism with $n$-sided ends has $3n$ edges.
solution: Pyramid: $2 \times 9 = 18$ edges. Prism: $3n = 18$, so $n = 6$. The prism is a hexagonal prism.

prompt: Explain the difference between a prism and a pyramid.
modelAnswer: A prism has two identical ends that are parallel to each other, joined by rectangular faces, so it has the same cross-section all the way through. A pyramid has only one base, and all its other faces are triangles that meet at a single point (the apex), so it gets narrower towards the top.

rubric.criterion: Prism: two identical (parallel) ends joined by rectangles, so the cross-section is the same all the way through

prompt: A box for one kiwifruit is a cuboid 8 cm long, 6 cm wide and 6 cm high. What is the total area of card in its net? (Ignore any flaps.)
hints: The net is made of 6 rectangles, in 3 matching pairs.
Find the area of each different rectangle, double each one, then add.
solution:
Top and bottom: $2 \times (8 \times 6) = 96$ cm².

Front and back: $2 \times (8 \times 6) = 96$ cm².

The two ends: $2 \times (6 \times 6) = 72$ cm².

Total area $= 96 + 96 + 72 = 264$ cm².

hints: Count the cube's edges first. Do any of them disappear when the pyramid is added?
How many new edges does the pyramid add?
solution:
The cube has 12 edges, and they are all still edges of the new solid (the 4 top edges are now where the cube's sides meet the pyramid's triangles). The pyramid adds 4 sloping edges that go up to its apex.

Total: $12 + 4 = 16$ edges.

Check with Euler's rule: faces $= 5 + 4 = 9$, vertices $= 8 + 1 = 9$, and $9 + 9 - 16 = 2$ ✓

prompt: Hemi says he has made a pyramid with 15 edges. Explain why this is impossible.
modelAnswer: If a pyramid's base has n sides, it has n edges around the base and n edges going up to the apex, so it has 2n edges altogether. 2n is always an even number, but 15 is odd. So no pyramid can have 15 edges.

rubric.criterion: Shows that a pyramid with an n-sided base has n + n = 2n edges (base edges plus edges up to the apex)
Explains that 2n is always even and 15 is odd, so it is impossible

hints: How many edges does a triangular pyramid have? A square-based pyramid?
If the base has $n$ sides, how many edges are around the base, and how many go up to the apex?
solution: A pyramid with an $n$-sided base has $n$ base edges and $n$ edges up to the apex, so it has $2n$ edges. That is always an **even** number (6, 8, 10, …). 15 is odd, so Hemi can't have made a pyramid with 15 edges.

prompt:
Two identical square-based pyramids are glued together at their square bases, so the squares are hidden inside the new solid. Complete the counts for the new solid.

Faces: [[f]]

Vertices: [[v]]

Edges: [[e]]
hints: Each pyramid has 4 triangular faces. The square bases are hidden inside.
The 4 corners of the square are shared by both pyramids, and each pyramid has its own apex.
solution:
Faces: $4 + 4 = 8$ triangles (the squares are glued together inside).

Vertices: the 4 corners of the square plus the 2 apexes $= 6$.

Edges: 4 around the square, 4 up to the top apex and 4 down to the bottom apex $= 12$.

Check: $8 + 6 - 12 = 2$ ✓ (This solid is called an octahedron.)

prompt:
One corner is sliced off a cube. The cut goes through three points, one part-way along each of the three edges that meet at that corner, and it makes a new triangular face. Complete the counts for the new solid.

Faces: [[f]]

Vertices: [[v]]

Edges: [[e]]
hints: The cut adds one new face. How many corners and edges does that triangle have?
One vertex of the cube is cut away, but each corner of the triangle is a new vertex.
solution:
Faces: $6 + 1 = 7$ (the 6 faces of the cube, plus the new triangle).

Vertices: the cube had 8. One is cut off, and the triangle adds 3 new ones: $8 - 1 + 3 = 10$.

Edges: all 12 edges of the cube are still there (three of them are just shorter), plus the 3 edges of the triangle: $12 + 3 = 15$.

Check: $7 + 10 - 15 = 2$ ✓
